newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Chiroscience focus on drug launch.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Chiroscience focus on drug launch.

text.p: British drug discoverer Chiroscience Group Plc is "totally focused" on the launch of its first major drug, the anaesthetic Levobupivacaine, chief executive John Padfield said on Monday.
In a telephone interview with Reuters, Padfield said,"this year is clearly going to be very important. Levobupivacaine is a key milestone for the company and we are totally focused on that".

He added that with recruitment of patients for 20 clinical trials of the drug progressing rapidly, he was "confident" that the group's target of filing for European approval in December would be achieved.
The company is aiming for a U.S. application in April 1998.
"Some U.S. trials have recruited more than half of their patients in less than six weeks, therefore we are confident that the December filing will be achieved," Padfield said.

Chiroscience has used its skills in chiral technology, which enable it to identify and remove elements of a drug responsible for side effects, to develop a purified version of an existing local anaesthetic, Bupivacaine.

Analysts expect the market for long-lasting anaesthetics to expand rapidly as the trend towards cheaper day surgery in hospitals continues. The drug is also likely to be used for controlling childbirth pain.

Analysts are waiting for the announcement of a marketing partner for Levobupivacaine. Padfield told Reuters that, given the potential range of uses for the drug, it might seek a number of partners, with room for "niche players" in areas like ophthalmology.
The company will also take a case-by-case approach for partnerships on its pipeline of more novel drugs, which Levobupivacaine should help to fund.
In asthma, where Chiroscience's PDE IV inhibitor is expected to start clinical trials next month, Padfield said major partners would be desirable.
"There are some very established players and you are talking about very expensive clinical trials to get this to the market," Padfield said.

However, in the area of MMP inhibitors, a new class of drugs which includes British Biotech Plc cancer treatment Marimastat, Padfield said British Biotech had shown it was "possible to take this on further without massive investment," allowing a bigger slice of the rewards to be kept.
Chiroscience has chosen two MMP inhibitor compounds for cancer, which Padfield said were expected to go into clinical trials "by the year-end."
Phase II trials of a drug for arthritis, which has run into technical problems in initial trials, "could start in the next nine months," Padfield said.

He said that beyond Levobupivacaine, the company's immediate aim was to give shareholders more information about Darwin Molecular, the Seattle-based gene company bought last December for $120 million.
"We want to get an indication back to shareholders of the value of what we have bought. That is another priority," said Padfield.
Chiroscience is to present a technology and research update which will include work at Darwin in London on May 30 and in New York on June 2.
